paragraphs.text: Y562 is the export code for a loose [ripe pu’er](shou:definition) from Yunnan, which drinkers nicknamed the [“little black box”](y562:little-black-box) after its carton. The Jixing mark on the front shows a tiger coming downhill. The box was made to carry the province’s [own brand](y562:export-trade). Much of Yunnan’s loose pu’er once travelled in bulk, and in Japan importers repacked it under their own labels. In 1980 Yunnan brought packaging and tea export designers together to change that, so Y562 carried Chinese lettering on the front and “Superior Yunnan Pu-erh Tea” on the back.

Tang Zheng drew the tiger from an openwork jade pendant, and Yin Huize framed the lettering with patterns taken from Chinese lacquerware. The two took cartons painted by hand to the spring [Canton Fair](y562:designers), and buyers ordered from those samples. Pu’er magazine describes the [original blend](y562:original-blend) as grades five and six of ripe tea from Menghai Tea Factory. Its yellow box companion, Y671, used grades six and seven from Kunming Tea Factory.

This box dates from 1993, twenty years after Yunnan’s state factories brought the [wet pile](shou:wet-piling) into production, which places it in the style’s third decade. At thirty-three years it counts as [aged ripe pu’er](shou:age-aged). The leaf keeps changing with the air and moisture around it, so its storage has shaped it as much as its age.

brewing.text: Ripe pu’er takes boiling water: fermented, tightly packed leaf needs full heat to open, and it does not scald the way green tea can. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and one quick rinse, which wakes the leaf and carries off dust and any pile smell. Then short steeps that lengthen as the leaf opens, so the cup stays clear rather than heavy; it gives eight or more good cups.

notice.text: A smooth, deep cup with woody, date-like or medicinal notes, which the trade calls aged aroma.
